Storage decisions look technical but are actually business-critical. The difference between good and bad storage shows up when something goes wrong, at which point it is too late to change the design.
- SAN (Storage Area Network): high-performance block storage, expensive, used for databases and virtualization
- NAS (Network Attached Storage): file-level storage, cheaper, used for shared drives and backups
- Cloud storage: object storage like S3, elastic and cheap but with different performance characteristics
- Backup: regular, tested, and separate from production. If you cannot restore it, you do not have a backup
- Disaster recovery: documented RTO and RPO targets, tested at least annually, automated where possible
## Hybrid cloud in real environments
Most enterprise infrastructure is hybrid, not pure cloud. Legacy systems often stay on-prem because of regulatory requirements, data gravity, or integration complexity. Our job is to make the on-prem and cloud sides work together cleanly, not to force everything into one or the other.
## Discovery questions
- What's the age of your current hardware, and when is the next refresh cycle?
- How many data centers, and are any leased with an upcoming renewal date?
- What percentage of your workloads are on-prem versus cloud today?
- When you had your last infrastructure-related outage, what caused it?
- Who currently manages your network, storage, and backup? In-house or outsourced?
## Common objections
- Objection: "Our infrastructure is fine" — Response: It works until the next hardware refresh or outage. Infrastructure problems compound slowly, so the conversation is about when, not if. We can run a short assessment that benchmarks your current state and identifies the top risks.
- Objection: "Everything is moving to cloud, so why invest on-prem?" — Response: Most customers end up hybrid for years, sometimes permanently. On-prem infrastructure still has to work, and the integration between on-prem and cloud is often the weakest link.
Key takeaway — Key positioning: Infrastructure is plumbing. Frame it as the foundation every other initiative depends on. Customers underinvest here until something breaks; our job is to help them see the risk before the break. Lead with an assessment that documents current state and identifies the top three risks.

Glossary:
- Server: A computer that provides services or resources to other computers. Can be physical hardware or a virtual machine.
- Virtualization: Running multiple virtual servers on a single piece of physical hardware. Increases efficiency and flexibility.
- VMware / Hyper-V: The two dominant virtualization platforms. VMware is popular across industries; Hyper-V is common in Microsoft-centric environments.
- Router: A network device that forwards data between networks. Connects your office to the internet.
- Switch: A network device that connects devices within the same network, like computers in an office.
- Firewall: A network device that filters traffic based on security rules. Protects networks from unwanted access.
- SAN (Storage Area Network): High-performance block storage for critical workloads like databases. Expensive but fast.
- NAS (Network Attached Storage): File-level storage shared across a network. Cheaper than SAN; used for shared drives and backups.
- Backup: Copies of data kept separately from production so data can be restored after a failure. Regular, tested, and ideally automated.
- DR (Disaster Recovery): Plans and systems for restoring operations after a major outage. Tested at least annually.
- Hybrid Cloud: A setup that uses both on-prem and cloud together. Most real enterprise infrastructure is hybrid today.
- Data Center: A physical facility where servers and networking equipment live. Often leased or cloud-replaced today.
- LAN (Local Area Network): A network within a limited area, like an office or building.
- WAN (Wide Area Network): A network that spans large geographic distances, connecting offices or data centers.
- VPN (Virtual Private Network): A secure tunnel over a public network. Used for remote access and connecting sites.

title: Migration Services
subtitle: O365, cloud, and infrastructure migrations
text:
Migration Services is one of our most concrete, easy-to-sell service lines because the customer's pain is visible: aging infrastructure, expiring contracts, or acquisitions that need to be integrated. Your job is to qualify which migration pattern applies, and lead with our 4-phase methodology to differentiate from generic competitors who just quote a headcount and a timeline.

## Understanding Migration Opportunities
- Microsoft 365 / G-Suite: Email, SharePoint, Teams, OneDrive. Productivity platform migrations and consolidations.
- Cloud Infrastructure: AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle. Workload migrations between or into the public cloud.
- Data Center Consolidation: On-prem to cloud or hybrid. Often driven by lease renewal or M&A.
## Why clients buy
- Cost Reduction: eliminate hardware refresh cycles and predictable monthly billing
- Business Continuity: better disaster recovery and geographic redundancy
- Scalability: pay-as-you-grow model, no capacity planning headaches
- Security: enterprise-grade protection without building it yourself
- Consolidation: one platform across an acquired organization or merged business units
## Red flags to listen for (trigger events)
Migration conversations rarely start with 'we want to migrate.' They start with these phrases. When you hear them, the opportunity is active.
- Our email server is 7+ years old: Aging infrastructure driving a forced decision. Often a wedge into a broader M365 or hybrid conversation.
- We are running out of storage: Scalability wall. Migration unlocks elastic storage without refresh-cycle costs.
- Our team cannot collaborate remotely: M365 or G-Suite conversation opens here. Often combined with identity modernization.
- Our DR plan is backing up to tape: Dated DR practice. Modern backup is cloud-based and tested regularly.
- We acquired a company (M&A): Post-M&A integration is one of the largest migration opportunities available. Fixed deadline, high stakes.
- Our cloud cost is too expensive: Cloud-to-cloud migration or cost optimization engagement is in play.
## SmarTek21 migration methodology: our 4-phase delivery model
This phased model is what differentiates us from generic competitors. Each phase has clear deliverables and exit criteria, so customers always know where they are in the program.
- Phase 1: Discovery (Weeks 1 to 2): Environment audit; Dependency mapping; Risk identification
- Phase 2: Planning (Weeks 3 to 4): Target architecture design; Migration wave planning; Cutover schedule
- Phase 3: Execution (Weeks 5 to 8): Pilot migration with test users; Migration in planned waves; 24/7 support during cutover
- Phase 4: Stabilization (Weeks 9 to 12): Post-migration support; User adoption training; Performance optimization
## Risk management in migrations
The biggest migration risks are not technical; they are organizational. Users not knowing what changed, data in unexpected places, integrations nobody documented. Our discovery phase is designed specifically to surface these before execution begins.
- Every migration has a documented rollback procedure before cutover
- Pilot with a small friendly group before moving broader user populations
- Communication plan covering what changes, when, and who to contact if something goes wrong
- Adoption training scheduled alongside the migration, not after
- Post-migration support window to catch issues users only discover days later
## Sales discovery framework
Every migration conversation follows the same three steps: discovery, positioning, next steps.
- Current state: Walk me through your current setup. How old is your environment? What systems and how many users?
- Pain points: What keeps you up at night? Any recent outages or data loss? What is driving the conversation now?
## Positioning SmarTek21
- Objection: "Worried about downtime" — Response: Our phased approach means under 2 hours total downtime across the whole migration, and most is planned during off-hours.
- Objection: "This sounds expensive" — Response: Cloud typically pays for itself in 18 to 24 months when you factor in hardware refresh avoidance and operational costs.
- Objection: "Too small for a migration" — Response: Cloud scales down too. There is no size too small to benefit, and smaller migrations are often cleaner because there is less to map.
- Objection: "Not in the budget" — Response: When is your next budget cycle? We can time the assessment so the proposal lands when decisions are being made.
- Objection: "We will DIY" — Response: We have done 100+ migrations. Your team focuses on your business; we focus on moving you without downtime. That is the trade.
Key takeaway — Next steps to offer: Position a FREE migration assessment. Timeline: 1 to 2 weeks for the assessment. Proposal delivered in 5 business days after. This low-friction opener is how most of our larger migration engagements begin.

Glossary:
- Migration: Moving systems, data, or applications from one environment to another. Common examples: email from Exchange to M365, workloads from on-prem to cloud.
- M365 (Microsoft 365): Microsoft's productivity cloud: Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive, Office apps. The dominant enterprise productivity suite.
- G-Suite / Google Workspace: Google's productivity cloud: Gmail, Drive, Docs, Meet. Microsoft's main competitor in this space.
- SharePoint: Microsoft's collaboration and document management platform. Often migrated alongside email.
- Teams: Microsoft's chat and meeting tool. Replaced Skype for Business in most enterprises.
- OneDrive: Microsoft's personal cloud file storage for M365 users.
- Cutover: The specific point in time when a migration goes live. Users are using the new system from this moment.
- Wave Migration: Moving users or workloads in planned groups (waves) rather than all at once. Reduces risk.
- Pilot: A small first migration to validate the approach before the full rollout. Typically a friendly group of users.
- Data Center: A physical facility where servers and networking equipment live. Many migrations eliminate on-prem data centers entirely.
- Lift and Shift: Moving workloads to cloud with minimal changes. The fastest migration path.
- DR (Disaster Recovery): Backup and recovery systems. Often improved as part of a cloud migration.
- M&A (Mergers and Acquisitions): When companies combine or one buys another. Post-M&A IT integration is a major migration driver.
- TCO (Total Cost of Ownership): All costs over a system's life. Migration business cases compare current TCO vs projected future TCO.
